newsitem.title: UK: Softs Outlook - Coffee in limbo, cocoa vulnerable.
newsitem.headline: Softs Outlook - Coffee in limbo, cocoa vulnerable.

text.p: Coffee's fortunes may remain in limbo this week after last week's dive to a 31-month-low on a fund sell-off while cocoa looks susceptible to further losses.

In white sugar, analysts ruled out much hope for the upside in the short term but activity was expected to pick up -- at least in terms of volume -- with the re-emergence of the New York market after its extended holiday break.
While New York was closed for Thanksgiving, commodity funds led a sell-off in London, pushing January coffee futures to the lowest since March 1994.
January ended the week at $1,336 a tonne after a low of $1,331 and against $1,424 a week ago.
The avalanche of selling orders also came from trade houses, origins and speculators ahead of the spot November contract's expiry on Friday.

While there were no fresh news or rumours driving the market, traders said the background fundamental picture for robusta coffee was far from bullish amid a seasonal rise in Asian and African production.
"Overall, the coffee picture is not that bullish, supplies are expected to come in from everywhere," said a trader with a U.S. trading house.
"On the demand side, buyers are well covered for December and January and could emerge to buy on the dips to cover their March requirements," he said. "It's a buyer's market."
Others said last week's selling could have been overdone and that there might be some upward technical correction.
Further market direction would hinge on fresh crop reports especially on key grower Brazil, traders said.

In sugar, the March white/raw premium would again be monitored closely and could easily narrow to around $60 as heavy overhead supply would pressure the whites while the raws would probably remain rangebound, traders and analysts said.

"It all looks shaky," one trader said. But March, the spot contract in both London and New York, might not be particularly active for the rest of the year as market players concerned with physical business would probably hold off until nearer delivery in the hope of lower prices.
"The problem that both markets have got is that once October is off the board, especially in New York, you've got such a long run until the next delivery," the broker said.
"People who have to do something in March won't even look at that position until the New Year," he said.
In cocoa, London's expiring December futures contract took the brunt of selling pressure late last week before its first tender day today.
"People are getting out of their long December positions," said one. A conviction that December cocoa would have a short validity period also weighed on the spot price.
In the immediate term, the market was looking at the arrivals from West African origins.
"That's bearing down the market, otherwise there's nothing much else to say about cocoa," he said. "I think the market is due to come lower. It's one-way traffic."
Cocoa's attempt to rack up further gains after recently jolting out of a downtrend had stalled at 943 stg a tonne, seen by analysts as a well-established chart barrier.
The technical rally was running out of steam, they said, and players were monitoring the verdict of crop forecasters on Ivory Coast's 1996/97 harvest after new arrivals figures became available.
Estimates were clustered around levels between 950,000 and one million tonnes for the total crop, but local exporters said the crop was unlikely to exceed 900,000 due to erratic weather.
